# Control: written cold from a one-paragraph brief, no voice file, no examples.

Every January the cold came down off the lake and sat on Maple Street for a month, and every morning Hollis stepped out the back door in his socks to shake the mat before he put his boots on. And every morning the kitchen door locked behind him. I heard it click from the stove. I'd look up from my coffee and there he'd be on the porch, knocking on the glass like a man at a bank window.

"Ruth," he'd say, through the pane. "Ruth, I'm standing in the snow."

"You're standing on the porch," I'd say, and get up slowly, because my hip had opinions about mornings, and turn the key the way the door wanted it turned. Some mornings it turned. Some mornings it turned only if I lifted the knob a little and leaned on it, and Hollis would say I was the only woman in Indiana who could open a door by moral persuasion.

We had the lock looked at twice. The man from Fort Wayne said the latch plate had shifted. The man from the hardware store said the house had settled, which I told him a house does not do in a single winter. He said it did in old houses. I said we were not that old. Hollis said nothing about it. He just bought a new strike plate and a can of graphite and tried both, and the door kept doing what it liked.

It was the library that gave me the answer, which I suppose is only fair. Mrs. Dorsey brought in a county bulletin about frost in old foundations, and I was shelving it when I read the line about heave: how the ground swells when the water in it freezes and lifts whatever sits on top. A concrete step is a poor thing to have sitting on frozen ground. It rises a little each winter and settles a little in spring, and a little is enough to bend a door out of true.

So that evening I said so at supper. Hollis chewed for a while, the way he does when he is turning something over.

"The back step," he said.

"The back step."

"It's come up." He put down his fork. "Ruth, it's come up a good inch under the frame. I felt it on the way out this morning and thought it was my socks."

We went out with the flashlight and the shovel. The snow had drifted against the step, and when Hollis brushed it away there was a dark wet patch on the concrete. The step sat crooked against the house, its near corner raised like a lid that had not quite closed. Right beside it, where the downspout ended in a stubby elbow of tin, the ground was soft and gray and glittering with ice. All winter the rain and the snowmelt had poured out of that spout, straight onto the one spot where the frost could get at the footing the most.

"Well, there's your culprit," I said.

"There's my culprit," Hollis said, and he laughed, which he does not do enough at six in the morning or at any hour of the day.

He fixed it that Saturday. He dug out the soft ground and packed it with gravel. Then he cut a length of drainage pipe and ran the downspout out past the end of the step and down to the grass, where the water could go somewhere else. He shimmed the step with flat stone and tamped it back level. Then he stood back and looked at it the way he looks at a letter that came out right.

"That'll hold," he said.

Monday morning he went out the back door, and I heard the old click of the latch, and I didn't get up. I waited. He went down the steps, and I heard his feet crunch along the path, and I thought, well, that's the end of that.

Then I heard him stop. Then I heard him laugh out loud in the cold. He came back up the step and knocked on the glass and said, "Ruth, I'm standing on a step that doesn't move."

I got up anyway. I turned the key, and the door swung open on its own hinges, easy as anything. He came in with the snow on his shoulders and the cold on his face, and he kissed me on the cheek with his cold nose. I told him he was letting the heat out. He said that was a fair price for a warm wife.
